subject: psychology
title: Working Memory Model: Evidence
welcome_lead: Dual-task studies, brain damage and word length — the case for WMM.
meta_desc: A-Level Psychology Working Memory Model evidence: dual-task, KF case, word length effect.
final_note: Evidence for the model is its real-world demonstrations of independent components.

concepts.def: Two tasks done together to test if they share resources.
Lists of short words easier to recall than long words.
Saying 'the the the' blocks phonological loop.
Shallice & Warrington patient with selective verbal STM damage.
Different WMM tasks activate different brain regions.
Prose recall in STM exceeds digit capacity — needs binding store.

walkthroughs.body_html: Baddeley et al. (1975) had participants do two visual tasks at once — performance dropped. Two tasks using different slave systems (visual + verbal) showed little interference. This dissociation supports separate components rather than a unitary STM.

Word length effect: people recall more short words ('cat', 'sun') than long words ('university', 'tuberculosis') — explained by the 2-second articulatory loop. Articulatory suppression (repeating 'the the the') prevents rehearsal and abolishes the word length effect — supporting the loop.

KF (Shallice & Warrington 1970) had a motorbike accident damaging his verbal STM but spared visual STM — STM must be multi-component. Modern fMRI: verbal tasks activate left frontal/temporal cortex; visuo-spatial tasks activate right hemisphere — different components, different brains.
